  1. Detect the problem and confirm its impact
  2. Assemble verified operational context
  3. Form an experience-led hypothesis
  4. Give AI a bounded reasoning task
  5. Validate the recommendation deterministically
  6. Pass through a human decision gate
  7. Execute, verify and roll back when required
  8. Capture the validated decision path
  9. Improve the operational skill through governed feedback
AI begins at Step 4. It does not own Steps 1 to 3, and it cannot cross Step 6 without explicit authority.

Phase 1: Problem Framing & Context Assembly

Step 1: Detect and scope the problem

The monitoring system reports increased errors and dropped traffic. The engineer first confirms customer impact, affected services and the time the failure began. A single application log is evidence, but it is not yet the incident context.

The incident owner opens a timeline, records the first known failure and pauses unrelated changes that could alter the evidence. The workflow proceeds only after the alert is confirmed against service-level indicators rather than accepted at face value.

Exit condition: The team knows what is failing, when it started and which customer path is affected.

Step 2: Assemble verified context

The engineer collects only authoritative evidence: the error signature, service metrics, deployment history, dependency health, current configuration, infrastructure state and recent policy changes. Each item comes from Git, telemetry, cloud APIs or another approved system of record.

The evidence package records source, timestamp and environment for every item. Sensitive values are removed, but identifiers needed for correlation remain. This prevents AI from comparing production logs with a staging configuration or an outdated policy snapshot.

Exit condition: The evidence package is current, traceable and free from guessed values.

Step 3: Form an experience-led hypothesis

The experienced engineer compares the evidence with known failure patterns. Suppose the error appeared immediately after the release, one dependency remains healthy and the failure affects only requests using a changed IAM path. The engineer forms a specific hypothesis: the release introduced a permission mismatch.

The hypothesis must state three things: the suspected cause, the observation expected if it is correct and the evidence that would disprove it. This converts experience into a testable decision rather than an intuition that cannot be challenged.

This step matters because AI should not receive an unbounded request such as, ‘Find the root cause.’ It should receive a testable engineering question.

Exit condition: The engineer has a hypothesis that can be proven or rejected.

Phase 2: Bounded Reasoning & Controlled Execution

Step 4: Give AI a bounded task

AI now enters the workflow. It receives the verified evidence, the proposed hypothesis and a narrow instruction: compare the deployed IAM configuration with the approved baseline, identify the smallest relevant difference and cite the evidence used.

The expected output is not a list of every possible cause. It follows a fixed response contract: finding, supporting evidence, confidence, missing information and a proposed verification command. Any claim without a cited input is treated as an assumption, not a fact.

Exit condition: AI has produced a falsifiable recommendation without performing a production change.

If the team skips these first four steps and sends a raw requirement directly to AI, the workflow usually becomes a correction loop:

Step 5: Validate deterministically

The proposed difference is checked against systems that produce repeatable results. The team compares Git with the deployed configuration, queries the live IAM policy, runs a policy test and confirms that the affected request path fails under the current permission set.

The validation sequence moves from lowest risk to highest confidence: syntax check, configuration diff, policy evaluation, dry run and a targeted test against the affected path. Each check produces a pass or fail result that can be attached to the incident record.

If the evidence does not support the recommendation, the workflow returns to Step 3 with the new facts. AI does not get permission to keep guessing until something works.

Exit condition: The root cause and proposed fix are supported by reproducible checks.

Step 6: Pass through the human decision gate

The engineer reviews the fix, blast radius, rollback action and expected recovery signal. The decision is explicit: approve, reject or request more evidence. Production authority remains with the accountable engineer or the established approval process.

The execution broker applies a compact risk rubric before any tool is allowed to act:

  • Read-only diagnostics: May run automatically when inputs are approved, actions are logged and no state can change.
  • Reversible, bounded changes: May run within pre-approved limits only when the target, blast radius, success check and tested rollback are explicit.
  • Stateful or destructive changes: Require explicit human approval. This includes actions affecting access, data, network exposure, cost or service availability.

This is the execution broker boundary: AI may prepare the action package, but authority is granted according to the tier, never inferred from confidence.

AI can recommend an action. It cannot accept the operational risk on behalf of the engineer.

Exit condition: An accountable owner has authorized a bounded change with a rollback path.

Step 7: Execute, verify and roll back when required

A deterministic script or approved runbook applies the minimal permission correction. The execution package contains the exact change, target environment, timeout, retry limit and rollback command. It must be idempotent so a repeated invocation cannot compound the impact.

The platform then checks the same signals used to scope the incident: error rate, request success, dependency health and customer impact. Recovery is declared only when the predefined success threshold remains stable for the agreed observation window.

Success ends the incident. Failure or an unexpected signal triggers the predefined rollback. AI may summarize the result, but the verification criteria were defined before execution.

Exit condition: Service health is restored and confirmed, or the change has been reversed safely.

Phase 3: Institutionalization & Governed Memory

Step 8: Capture the validated decision path

The team records the reusable parts of the resolution: trigger, required evidence, decision rule, approved action, verification checks, rollback conditions and owner. False leads and conversational noise are removed.

The skill has a clear contract: accepted inputs, preconditions, allowed tools, prohibited actions, maximum blast radius, success criteria, rollback procedure and audit output. If a precondition is missing, the skill stops and requests evidence instead of improvising.

The result is a repeatable operational skill. Deterministic components collect evidence and execute approved actions. AI handles variable inputs such as log wording, correlation and matching the current symptoms with the correct skill.

Exit condition: Another engineer can run the skill without depending on the original responder’s memory.

Step 9: Improve through governed feedback

Each use records whether the diagnosis was correct, whether the action restored service, how long recovery took and which exceptions occurred. The team tracks false positives, operator overrides, rollback frequency and time saved. AI may propose an updated rule or new evidence requirement from those outcomes.

The skill does not rewrite itself in production. Proposed changes are replayed against historical incidents, reviewed by experienced engineers, versioned and approved before release.

Exit condition: Improvement is evidence-based, tested and accountable.

One resolution becomes automation. Repeated validated resolutions become a skill. Governed feedback improves the skill.

My friend returned to the original question. “So where does AI actually start and stop?”

It starts after impact is understood, evidence is verified and an experienced engineer has framed a testable problem. It stops before risk is accepted, production authority is exercised or success is declared.

Between those boundaries, AI can analyze evidence, compare patterns, propose minimal changes and help select a validated operational skill.

Experience is not replaced. It defines the workflow, controls the boundary and converts successful judgment into reusable capability.

The best engineering teams will not be those that use the most AI. They will be those that know exactly where AI belongs in the workflow and can prove that the workflow works.

title: The Phone Is Not Just Taking Our Time. It Is Taking Our Presence.
body:
We blame the job. The business. The meetings. The commute. The bills. The endless responsibilities that come with being an adult.

All of that may be true.

But there is one energy drainer we carry everywhere. It is in our hand, pocket, bedroom, dining table, car and sometimes even beside our child while they are trying to talk to us.

The phone.

The strange part is that it does not always look like a problem. We are not doing anything “wrong”. We are reading news. Checking messages. Watching one short video. Looking at updates. Learning something. Staying informed.

Even this article is reaching you through the same system that drains your attention.

That is the uncomfortable contradiction of modern life.

Technology is necessary. It connects families, businesses, classrooms, hospitals, banks and almost every serious system around us. I am not arguing against technology. That would be unrealistic.

The question is different.

After what point does useful technology become constant mental consumption?

Psychology gives us a useful lens here. Our brain was not designed to process an endless stream of alerts, opinions, comparisons, bad news, good news, breaking news, forwarded advice and random entertainment without cost. Attention is not unlimited. Every feed asks the mind to shift, react, judge, compare or worry.

The American Psychological Association has discussed how constant checking of devices is associated with higher stress. Another American Psychological Association article points to notifications as one source of distraction and mental pressure.

  • The issue is not only screen time.
  • It is interruption time.
  • It is the repeated breaking of attention.

When we were children, information had natural boundaries.

A newspaper ended. A book had pages. A conversation with a friend over a board game had a beginning and an end. A coffee discussion ended when people got up and went home.

Today, the feed does not end.

That changes adults. But it may be changing children even more deeply.

The American Psychological Association’s advisory on adolescent social media use explains that social media is not simply good or bad for young people. Its impact depends on the child, the content, the amount of use and the child’s developmental stage.

As parents, how many times have we felt that a child is “zoned out”? Sometimes they are tired. Sometimes they are bored. Sometimes they are simply growing.

But increasingly, many children are not zoning out into imagination, silence, outdoor play or conversation. They are zoning out into the internet.

Switch off the internet at home for one hour, and many of us will quickly see how dependent the household has become on constant stimulation.

Many children do not know what to do with unstructured time.

That should worry us.

Not because children are weak. Because we are slowly removing the conditions that build strength.

A child needs movement, sunlight, boredom, small risks, physical play, arguments with friends, laughter, falling down, getting up, walking beside a parent, helping at home and learning how the real world feels.

Many of us live in gated communities with amenities everywhere. We may feel everything is available: play area, swimming pool, clubhouse, screens, classes and safety.

But availability is not the same as childhood.

Children still need active stimulation. They need parents who initiate walks, games, conversations and outdoor time. They need bodies that are used, not only minds that are entertained.

A simple run once ended with my son fracturing his hand. That moment hit me hard. It made me ask a question I was not fully ready for:

Am I raising my child to be comfortable, or capable?

I am still learning.

The answer is not to throw away phones, shame children or pretend we can return to an old world. The answer is to design better boundaries.

Maybe it starts small:

  • No phones during meals.
  • No phone beside the bed.
  • One family walk without devices.
  • One evening where boredom is allowed.
  • One board game.
  • One hour where the child sees the parent not scrolling.
  • One conversation where we listen without checking a notification.

The American Academy of Pediatrics encourages families to think in terms of balance, routines and healthy behaviors rather than only one fixed screen-time number. The World Health Organization also emphasizes physical activity and reducing sedentary time as part of health across age groups.

That feels practical.

We do not need perfect parenting. We need conscious parenting.

We cannot ask children to build attention while we constantly surrender ours. We cannot ask them to love outdoor play if we never step out with them. We cannot ask them to speak openly if our eyes keep moving back to a screen.

Technology will keep advancing. It should.

But our responsibility must also advance.

As adults, we need to ask what our devices are taking from us in small invisible payments: attention, sleep, patience, silence, movement, presence and sometimes even our relationship with our children.

I am not writing this as someone who has solved it. I am writing this as a parent who is learning.

Because children do not remember the posts we read, the notifications we cleared or the emails we answered in record time.

They remember whether we looked up when they called our name.

Setting down the phone will not solve every complexity of modern parenting. But it restores the one thing technology constantly tries to steal: the quiet, unscripted moments where real childhood happens.

The next generation does not just need better technology.

They need parents who are fully present to watch them grow.

title: From ChatGPT and Codex to an Agentic Terraform Platform
dek: What repeated infrastructure work taught me about deterministic discovery, probabilistic reasoning, guardrails, and keeping humans in…
heroCaption: From AI-assisted infrastructure work to a guarded agentic engineering platform.
body:
What repeated infrastructure work taught me about deterministic discovery, probabilistic reasoning, guardrails, and keeping humans in control

Infrastructure automation has traditionally been deterministic.

  • We write code.
  • We validate it.
  • We generate a plan.
  • We review the changes.
  • We apply them.

Then generative AI entered the engineering workflow.

Suddenly, an engineer could describe a requirement in natural language and ask an AI system to reason about Terraform, troubleshoot cloud infrastructure, propose configuration changes, interpret errors, and even modify a repository.

That is incredibly powerful. It is also where things get interesting.

Over time, as I used ChatGPT and Codex across repeated infrastructure engineering activities, I realized that the important question was no longer:

Can an LLM write Terraform?

Clearly, it can. The more important question became:

What controls do we need before we can responsibly allow AI to participate in infrastructure engineering?

That question eventually pushed me toward something much larger than AI-assisted Terraform development. I started thinking about an agentic infrastructure engineering platform.

Not an autonomous bot with unrestricted cloud access. Not a chatbot that generates Terraform and immediately runs it. Instead, an evidence-driven system where AI reasons over verified infrastructure facts, deterministic software enforces policy, Terraform remains the execution authority, and engineers retain control over consequential actions.

That distinction has shaped almost every design decision since.

It Started With a Very Repetitive Engineering Loop

The starting point was surprisingly ordinary.

An infrastructure baseline had been designed and reviewed. Then application development continued. New requirements kept arriving, requests any platform or cloud engineer will recognize: enable an optional managed service, add a new application dependency, introduce service-to-service communication, add private connectivity, expose another application capability, update environment-specific configuration, add an identity or permission, modify network connectivity.

Individually, none of these requests was particularly difficult. The challenge was the repetition. Almost every requirement triggered the same engineering cycle:

Understand the requirement → inspect existing Terraform → inspect current infrastructure → understand dependencies → determine the smallest safe change → modify Terraform → terraform fmt → terraform validate → terraform plan → review the impact → obtain approval → apply → validate the actual environment → communicate the outcome.

At first, I used ChatGPT as a reasoning partner throughout this workflow. Then I started using coding agents such as Codex to work more directly with the repository.

Eventually, something became obvious. I was not solving isolated Terraform problems anymore. I was repeatedly executing the same infrastructure engineering process. That led to a different question:

Instead of asking an AI assistant to help me perform this workflow every time, can the workflow itself become a guarded agentic platform?

That became the real project.

Why ChatGPT Was Useful

Cloud infrastructure failures rarely arrive with clean boundaries. An application might report a connectivity failure, but the actual cause could be DNS, routing, private networking, identity, RBAC, application configuration, Terraform drift, a managed service, CI/CD, security policy, or an incorrect environment reference.

This is where conversational reasoning became particularly useful. Rather than immediately changing infrastructure, I could work through a dependency chain: does the target resource exist, does private connectivity exist, does DNS resolve correctly, can the workload reach the endpoint, is the runtime configuration correct, does the workload identity have access. Each verified result removes another category of possible causes.

The value of AI in this situation was not that it magically knew the answer. The value was that it helped maintain context, generate useful hypotheses, interpret command output, and progressively turn assumptions into evidence.

But conversational reasoning had an obvious limitation. It could tell me what I might need to change. I still needed to safely change the repository. That is where Codex became important.

Why I Picked Codex

Infrastructure engineering is repository-centric. Once a Terraform implementation exists, the question is rarely:

How do I create this resource?

Clearly, it can. The better question is:

Given the architecture that already exists, what is the smallest safe change required to satisfy this new requirement?

The repository contains far more than HCL syntax, it contains architectural intent: main.tf, variables.tf, terraform.tfvars, outputs.tf, providers.tf, and modules for compute, networking, security, data, observability, and edge.

Inside that structure are decisions about naming, modules, environments, network topology, IP allocation, identity, private connectivity, security, feature flags, observability, dependencies, and ownership boundaries.

Those decisions may already have gone through architecture and security review. I do not want an AI system redesigning them every time a new requirement arrives. I want it to understand them.

A repository-aware coding agent therefore became valuable because it could operate closer to the real engineering artifact. But even repository awareness was not enough. That became clear when I started experimenting with smaller local models.

The Failure That Changed the Architecture

One experiment became particularly instructive. I gave a small local model a simple requirement:

Enable an optional infrastructure capability that already exists in the Terraform design.

The repository already contained a disabled feature flag and the implementation behind it. The correct process should have been straightforward:

Search for the capability, find the existing feature flag, trace where the variable is used, identify the resources controlled by it, inspect Terraform state, inspect actual cloud state, determine whether enabling the flag is sufficient, and generate a Terraform plan.

Instead, the model began requesting implementation parameters that were not actually required. In other words, it started constructing a solution before fully understanding the existing one.

This initially looked like a model-quality problem. It wasn’t. It was an architecture problem. I was asking an LLM to discover facts that software could discover deterministically. That realization produced what is now one of the central principles of the platform.

Discovery Should Be Deterministic. Reasoning Can Be Probabilistic.

An LLM should not have to guess whether a Terraform variable exists, search the repository. It should not guess whether a module already implements a capability, inspect the module graph. It should not guess whether a resource is already managed, query Terraform state. It should not guess which cloud account is active, ask the cloud API. It should not invent an IP range, query the approved network/IPAM source. It should not infer an ownership boundary when that boundary can be represented as policy.

Give the model facts. Then let it reason.

The architecture therefore starts looking less like a straight line from prompt to LLM to Terraform, and more like a pipeline: a developer requirement goes through requirement analysis, then deterministic discovery, pulling from the Terraform configuration, variables and locals, modules, resources, count/for_each, feature flags, dependencies, Terraform state, cloud APIs, network/IPAM, and organizational policy, which produces verified evidence. Only then does LLM reasoning propose a minimal delta, which passes through deterministic guardrails to become a Terraform plan, which a human approves.

This separation matters enormously. The LLM remains probabilistic. The infrastructure facts do not have to be.

LLM Confidence Is Not Evidence

This distinction deserves special attention. Suppose an LLM says:

This resource probably requires private connectivity.

That is reasoning. It may be excellent reasoning. But it is not evidence.

If the Terraform repository contains an explicit private-connectivity setting, that is evidence. If terraform state list shows the corresponding resource address, that is evidence. If the cloud API confirms that the private endpoint exists, that is evidence. If the organization’s network source identifies a particular subnet as the approved private-endpoint subnet, that is evidence.

The platform should preserve those distinctions. A reasoning engine should ideally be able to say “I recommend this change because of evidence A, B and C” rather than “this configuration looks reasonable.” That is a very different standard.

Three Types of Infrastructure Truth

An infrastructure agent often has to reconcile at least three different representations of reality.

Desired State

What the repository says should exist: Terraform configuration, variables, modules, policies, Git history.

Terraform-Known State

What Terraform believes it manages: Terraform state, resource addresses, provider state, dependencies, outputs.

Actual Cloud State

What is really running: cloud APIs, resource configuration, DNS, networking, identity, health, runtime configuration.

These three views may disagree. That disagreement is often where the most interesting engineering problems live.

Terraform Plan Became the Truth Boundary

One of the strongest lessons from using AI around infrastructure was that the model’s proposed change is not the final truth. The Terraform plan is.

Imagine an infrastructure change that has nothing to do with application deployment. The plan unexpectedly shows an application artifact changing because Terraform contains an older value while CI/CD has already deployed a newer one. The requested infrastructure change may be perfectly correct. The plan is still unsafe.

That reveals something important:

Infrastructure safety is not only about whether the requested change is correct. It is also about whether anything else changes with it.

This also exposes ownership boundaries: Terraform owns infrastructure configuration, CI/CD owns application releases, the identity platform owns selected credentials, the network platform owns shared network allocations, and security policy owns organizational controls.

An agent must understand these boundaries. Otherwise, technically valid Terraform can still create operationally incorrect outcomes.

Why I Don’t Want an LLM Running Shell Commands Freely

Another design decision followed naturally. If the LLM is probabilistic, why give it unrestricted shell access? Instead, I prefer an execution broker: the model requests a capability, and deterministic software decides whether that capability exists and whether the current workflow allows it.

  • Allowed: terraform fmt, terraform validate, terraform plan, terraform show, terraform state list, cloud read operations
  • Denied: arbitrary shell access, terraform destroy
  • Requires approval: terraform apply

The model expresses intent. Software maps that intent to a constrained capability. This substantially reduces the blast radius of a bad model decision.

Preflight Before Intelligence

The same philosophy applies before reasoning even starts. An agent should not assume that the machine executing it has the required access. This becomes particularly important when the same platform may run on a developer laptop, an engineering workstation, a CI runner, or an enterprise automation host.

Before calling an LLM, the platform can perform a deterministic preflight, checking that Terraform is installed and at a supported version, the cloud CLI is installed and authenticated, the correct account or tenant is active and the subscription is accessible, Git is available and the repository is readable, the repository matches the target environment, the Terraform backend is accessible and state is readable, and the LLM provider is reachable.

If a mandatory check fails, say, the backend state cannot be accessed, the platform fails closed: no infrastructure design generated, no Terraform plan generated, no cloud changes made.

This is deliberately conservative. For infrastructure engineering, conservative defaults are useful.

There Should Be Another Gate Before Apply

Passing preflight does not mean an agent should be able to apply indefinitely. Time passes. Repositories change. Credentials expire. State changes. Someone else may modify infrastructure.

So the system should perform another gate immediately before execution, confirming that the approval is still valid, the approved plan exists, the plan’s SHA-256 hash is unchanged, the workspace is unchanged, the cloud identity is valid, the backend is writable, and the required RBAC is valid. Only then does it run terraform apply against the approved plan file.

This leads to another important principle.

Approve the Artifact, Not the Intention

An engineer approving a natural-language request is not sufficient. The engineer should approve the actual Terraform plan, and the thing executed should be the same artifact.

The flow is: terraform plan produces an approved.tfplan file, which is hashed with SHA-256, reviewed by a human, and approved. Before execution, the SHA-256 is verified again, and only then does terraform apply run against that exact approved.tfplan.

The reviewed plan and the executed plan are therefore cryptographically tied together. That is a much stronger control boundary.

Human in the Loop Does Not Mean Human Does Everything

This is an important distinction. I am not trying to remove engineers from infrastructure decisions. I am trying to move them to the decisions where human judgment matters most.

Instead of manually searching dozens of files, tracing variables, checking state, copying CLI output, generating repetitive Terraform, formatting files, and assembling plan summaries, the engineer can review the requirement, the evidence, the affected resources, the proposed code diff, the Terraform plan, the risk classification, the policy results, and the validation strategy, then decide to approve, reject, or request changes.

The machine handles repetition. The engineer retains authority. That is what “human in the loop” should mean in this context.

Local Models and Cloud Models Can Coexist

Another goal was to avoid tying the platform to one model. A lightweight engineering environment may benefit from a local model. Complex infrastructure reasoning may benefit from a stronger hosted model. So the reasoning layer should be provider-agnostic: both local and hosted models feed the same reasoning layer, pass through the same guardrails, and produce the same kind of Terraform plan.

The model may change. The safety architecture should not. A larger model does not get additional Terraform privileges. A local model does not bypass policy. Every model operates behind the same execution boundary.

This also creates an interesting future capability: model routing. Routine classification might use a small local model. Complex architectural reasoning might be escalated to a stronger model. The platform can optimize for accuracy, latency, cost, privacy, and availability without redesigning the infrastructure workflow.

Sharing the Platform Without Sharing Secrets

Once an infrastructure tool becomes useful, other engineers will want to run it. That immediately creates a security problem, because infrastructure tooling interacts with cloud credentials, Git credentials, LLM API keys, state backends, CI/CD systems, registries, and secrets platforms. Those credentials should not travel with the source code.

A better structure keeps the repository, application code, Terraform, policies, configuration schema, startup scripts, and a .env.example, separate from the runtime environment and secret store, which holds the actual cloud credentials, LLM credentials, Git credentials, CI/CD credentials, and other runtime secrets.

Where possible, identity-based authentication is preferable: an engineer authenticates through enterprise identity, receives short-lived credentials, and is granted RBAC to cloud, Terraform state, and source control, instead of a shared tool holding one permanent super-credential to everything.

This has another advantage. Actions remain attributable to the identity that actually performed them. That is important for auditability.

From Chat Message to Infrastructure Transaction

The platform also changed how I think about infrastructure requirements. A request should not remain an unstructured chat message. It should become an infrastructure transaction, for example:

CHANGE-1042: Enable an existing optional platform capability, in a non-production environment. Discovery found an existing feature flag, confirmed the implementation already exists, and identified dependencies. The current Terraform state and actual cloud resources were both inspected. The proposed change was a single configuration value. The plan showed 3 to create, 1 to update, 0 to destroy. Guardrails passed: destroy protection, replacement protection, environment isolation, network policy, ownership boundaries, and secrets policy. The change was approved, the exact approved plan was executed, and validation confirmed the resources were healthy with connectivity and configuration verified. Status: completed.

Now the requirement has evidence, a decision, an artifact, an approval, an execution record, validation, and an outcome. That is much closer to an engineering control system than a chatbot.

What I Am Building Around This

The current implementation is intentionally lightweight. The larger direction is an agentic infrastructure engineering platform. I think of it in five layers, each with a different responsibility:

  • Experience layer: Requirements, plans, approvals, runs
  • Agent layer: Requirement, Terraform, cloud, network, security, planner, reviewer, and validator agents
  • Evidence layer: Git, state, cloud, IPAM, architecture, policy, ownership, and historical outcomes
  • Control plane: Guardrails, approval, tool broker, plan hash, RBAC, audit
  • Execution layer: Terraform, cloud APIs, CI/CD

That separation is intentional.

Requirement Intelligence

Infrastructure requests arrive through many channels: tickets, email, chat, meetings, architecture documents, and developer conversations. The first agent should normalize that request into structured intent, requested capability, target environment, affected systems, known constraints, dependencies, risk category, and missing information.

The system should distinguish between “I don’t understand the requirement” and “I understand the requirement, but a required infrastructure fact is missing.” Those are different failure modes.

Terraform Discovery

The Terraform agent’s first responsibility should not be generating HCL. It should understand the HCL that already exists, tracing variables, locals, modules, resources, outputs, providers, count, for_each, feature flags, dependencies, and state addresses.

A mature implementation could move beyond keyword search toward HCL parsing, Terraform AST analysis, module dependency graphs, resource relationship graphs, and state-to-code mapping. The output is not Terraform. The output is evidence about Terraform.

Cloud Discovery

Terraform describes desired state. The cloud describes actual state. A cloud discovery agent can inspect resource configuration, identity, RBAC, networking, DNS, managed services, private connectivity, runtime health, observability, and policy. This allows the platform to detect drift and reconcile infrastructure intent with reality.

Network and IPAM Intelligence

Networking deserves its own reasoning boundary. An infrastructure agent should understand network topology, subnet purpose, CIDR allocation, reserved addresses, private endpoint ranges, DNS relationships, routing, and security boundaries.

Before proposing an IP address, it should query an authoritative source. Before proposing a subnet, it should understand the topology. Before exposing a public endpoint, it should evaluate policy. This is an area where hallucination is particularly dangerous, syntactically valid networking is not necessarily operationally valid networking.

Guardrail and Policy Engine

The production safety model should live primarily outside the LLM. Deterministic controls should:

  • Deny resource destruction unless explicitly authorized
  • Deny replacement unless explicitly authorized
  • Deny cross-environment dependencies
  • Deny plaintext secrets
  • Deny unapproved public exposure
  • Deny unknown network ranges
  • Deny application artifacts owned by CI/CD
  • Deny resources outside approved scope
  • Deny execution when required evidence is missing

The model can explain why a policy failed. It cannot override the policy.

Multi-Agent Reasoning

Eventually, I do not expect one model invocation to own the entire workflow. A mature platform could use specialized agents in sequence: a requirement agent, then Terraform discovery, cloud discovery, and network agents, then an infrastructure designer, a security reviewer, a Terraform reviewer, a plan reviewer, and finally a validation agent.

The important word here is not multi-agent. It is specialization. Each component should have a defined purpose, constrained tools, specific evidence, explicit outputs, and deterministic boundaries. Otherwise, multiple agents simply create multiple opportunities for hallucination.

Post-Deployment Validation

A successful Terraform apply is not the same thing as a successful infrastructure change. Terraform may report “Apply complete!” while the application is still unhealthy.

Post-deployment validation should therefore be first-class, covering resource provisioning state, DNS resolution, TCP connectivity, private endpoint status, identity assignment, RBAC, health probes, application configuration, service availability, logs, and metrics.

The platform should be capable of saying “Terraform execution succeeded, but the desired operational outcome was not achieved.” That is much more useful than reporting only execution status.

Infrastructure Memory: But With a Critical Constraint

One of the most interesting possibilities is allowing the platform to learn from previous work. But “self-learning” can become dangerous very quickly. I do not want the system to store whatever the LLM generated and treat it as truth next time.

Instead, the path to memory runs through the full chain: requirement, evidence, decision, Terraform plan, approval, execution, validation, and outcome, only then does something become approved knowledge. Only validated outcomes should be candidates for long-term memory, and some knowledge should still require explicit approval: an observed pattern must be validated repeatedly and reviewed by an engineer before it becomes an approved organizational pattern and reusable knowledge.

This gives the platform memory without allowing hallucinations to become institutional knowledge.

The Platform Should Become Smarter Without Becoming More Autonomous

This is an important distinction. There is a tendency to measure agent maturity by how much human involvement can be removed. I think infrastructure requires a different metric:

How much manual effort can we remove while preserving or increasing control?

The platform can become dramatically smarter at discovering infrastructure, correlating evidence, proposing changes, identifying risks, generating plans, validating outcomes, and retrieving previous patterns — without automatically gaining permission to perform more consequential actions.

Intelligence and authority should be separate dimensions. That is a principle I intend to keep.

What Made the Original Workflow Successful?

Looking back, no single AI tool completed the activity. Different systems played different roles.

ChatGPT

Reasoning, troubleshooting, interpreting errors, generating diagnostic steps, maintaining context, evaluating alternatives, and communicating outcomes.

Codex

Repository-aware engineering, modifying Terraform, refactoring code, building the surrounding automation, and iterating quickly on the platform itself.

Terraform

Desired state, dependency resolution, change calculation, planning, and execution.

Cloud APIs and CLI Tools

Actual resource state, connectivity, runtime configuration, identity, and operational validation.

Humans

Intent, architecture, risk acceptance, approvals, and exceptions.

The workflow succeeded because those responsibilities were separated. Not because AI replaced all of them.

This Is Not About AI-Generated Terraform

That is perhaps the biggest change in how I think about this project. The interesting problem is no longer “can AI generate Terraform?” That capability is already here.

The interesting problems are:

Can AI understand what already exists? Can every recommendation be traced back to evidence? Can we constrain what the model is allowed to change? Can we prove that the plan being executed is the plan a human approved? Can we validate the operational outcome after Terraform finishes? Can the platform learn from validated history without turning hallucinations into organizational knowledge?

Those are much harder problems. And, in my view, much more valuable ones.

Final Thought

Using ChatGPT and Codex certainly made me faster. But speed was not the most important outcome.

The most important lesson was discovering where AI should stop. The safest architecture was not the architecture where the model had the most authority. It was the architecture where the model had access to the best evidence while deterministic systems controlled execution.

That has led me to a simple principle for agentic infrastructure engineering:

Let AI reason broadly. Let software verify aggressively. Let Terraform describe the change. Let policy define the boundary. And let humans authorize consequential actions.

What started as “can ChatGPT help me make this Terraform change?” has gradually become “what would a trustworthy agentic control plane around infrastructure engineering look like?” That is what I am building now. And I think that question is far more interesting.

Closing Note

This is an ongoing engineering experiment. The next stages include deeper Terraform graph analysis, infrastructure evidence models, policy-as-code integration, network/IPAM intelligence, multiple specialized agents, model routing, exact-plan approval workflows, post-deployment validation, and controlled infrastructure memory.

If you’re exploring AI-assisted DevOps, Terraform automation, platform engineering, or infrastructure agents, I would be interested in comparing approaches.

title: Why I Chose IB for My Kids Even Though I Grew Up in the Indian Curriculum System
dek: The Education Debate Every Parent in India Is Quietly Having
body:
The Education Debate Every Parent in India Is Quietly Having

If you follow the current discourse around school education in India, you have probably noticed how intense the conversations have become around CBSE, curriculum structures, evaluation discrepancies, and the growing preference for international boards like IB and Cambridge.

For many families, this is no longer a casual discussion. It is becoming a serious, long-term systems decision. And honestly, I never expected myself to be part of this conversation.

I grew up in the traditional Indian education system. Like many people from our generation, I was taught discipline, consistency, examination rigor, and academic persistence. Those foundations absolutely helped shape my career.

But somewhere along the way, I also realized something uncomfortable: A large percentage of the skills I rely on professionally today were not learned in school. I learned them painfully later in life.

The Pandemic Changed the Equation for Our Family

When the pandemic lockdowns disrupted the foundational learning years for millions of children, my son was directly affected. Like many parents, we saw the impact firsthand:

  • Reduced classroom interaction
  • Limited social learning
  • Interrupted communication development
  • Lower confidence in structured academic environments

At that point, we had a difficult decision to make. Do we push him immediately into a rigid academic system heavily optimized around writing, textbooks, assessments, and structured performance? Or do we place him in an environment that gives him space to rebuild gradually?

That was the primary reason we chose the IB Primary Years Programme (IB-PYP).

Not because we believed international curriculum were automatically “better,” and certainly not because we wanted educational branding. It was because, at that stage, it genuinely felt like the environment most aligned with where he was developmentally after the lockdown years. The emphasis on exploration, communication, collaboration, conceptual understanding, and experiential learning gave him necessary breathing room.

Initially, I thought this was just a temporary adjustment. But over time, the experience triggered a much deeper realization in me.

The Skills I Had to Learn 20 Years Late

Watching my children grow inside an experiential learning environment forced me to reflect on my own schooling journey. And honestly, I realized I spent almost twenty years manually correcting gaps that traditional education never addressed for me.

School taught me how to memorize. It taught me how to clear exams. It taught me how to survive academic pressure. But it did not prepare me for:

  • Public speaking and audience engagement
  • Professional presentations and storytelling
  • Open-ended research under pressure
  • Independent thinking and collaborative problem-solving

My stage fright was intense. I only started becoming comfortable speaking publicly nearly seven years into my professional career. Everything from presentation skills to communication confidence was learned through repeated exposure, failures, uncomfortable meetings, technical presentations, leadership interactions, and years of real-world experience.

That realization hit me hard because I started seeing my children naturally developing some of these capabilities much earlier.

The Financial Trade-Off Nobody Likes Talking About

But then comes the difficult part: the cost.

A traditional Indian curriculum can easily cost 50% less, sometimes even far lower, compared to international frameworks. That creates a very real, high-stakes dilemma for parents. Especially for people who look at family planning through a structural lens.

In fact, we personally chose to compromise on so many baseline lifestyle milestones just so we could continue to afford this journey. What started as a tactical choice to help my son find his footing after the lockdown has now become a sustained family commitment, as we continue the exact same IB path for my daughter.

When I look at that compounding investment, the engineer in me keeps returning to the same core question:

Is the lower cost of a legacy path truly cheaper if the model still depends heavily on rote learning, static textbooks, and examination-centric progression? Or is the extreme lifestyle premium justified if it directly accelerates confidence, critical thinking, and adaptability much earlier in life?

I honestly do not have a perfect, universal answer because this is not simply an academic decision. It is a calculated economic trade-off, a deep emotional choice, and increasingly, a future-of-work decision.

Evolving Ecosystems: Living in Bangalore, Karnataka

Living and working in Bangalore, Karnataka adds a very distinct, localized layer of complexity to this entire choices matrix.

On one hand, this city is the technical and entrepreneurial heartbeat of the country, our entire professional ecosystem thrives on adaptability, cloud-native infrastructure, and rapid innovation. On the other hand, our local educational policy landscape has been in a state of continuous transition.

Karnataka was actually one of the earliest states to formally adopt the National Education Policy (NEP 2020) around the 2021–22 timeframe. The intent was incredibly ambitious: move beyond rote learning and introduce multidisciplinary, skill-oriented, and experiential approaches into mainstream education. However, over the following years, Karnataka shifted direction, moving toward establishing its own State Education Policy (SEP) tailored around state-specific educational, regional, and linguistic priorities.

As a parent navigating school admissions and curriculum frameworks in Bangalore, this creates an underlying layer of system uncertainty. We are trying to figure out what the long-term educational operating system of the state will eventually look like.

At the same time, there are encouraging signs across the country. We are seeing active, phased implementations of these frameworks in states like Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, and Chhattisgarh, alongside targeted model school rollouts under the PM SHRI initiative in regions like Odisha and Haryana.(Information from Google Search)

These NEP-aligned initiatives are systematically introducing:

  • Competency-Based Assessments: Moving away from rote testing to measure true understanding, ensuring students master core concepts before advancing rather than just memorizing for an exam.
  • Activity-Driven Classrooms: Turning passive listeners into active participants, which drastically improves student engagement and information retention.
  • Experiential Learning Models: Allowing kids to learn by doing, bridging the massive gap between abstract textbook theories and real-world execution.
  • Multidisciplinary Exposure & Communication-Focused Learning: Giving students the early tools to build public confidence, express original ideas, and break free from the early stage fright that historically slowed down our generation when entering the corporate workforce.

PM SHRI schools, in particular, are actively demonstrating that a holistic education environment can be scaled within the public framework. Living in the tech capital, I genuinely hope Bangalore leverages its innovation ecosystem to become a true pioneer in this evolution. The real solution to our education crisis cannot be a binary choice where families are forced to either stretch financially for expensive international schools or watch their children navigate the same outdated, rote-learning pipeline we went through. True transformation means making high-quality, experiential learning both accessible and affordable at scale.

We Cannot Prepare Children for the Future Using Legacy Systems

The world our children are entering is fundamentally different from the one we grew up in.

  • AI is reshaping work.
  • Communication matters more than memorization.
  • Adaptability matters more than static knowledge.
  • Research capability matters more than textbook reproduction.
  • Problem-solving matters more than exam optimization.

Yet much of the educational infrastructure still resembles systems designed for a completely different economic era. That mismatch worries me. Not as a technologist, but as a parent.

Parenting Still Matters More Than Curriculum

At the same time, I do not believe any curriculum alone can solve this problem. No board can replace parenting.

Our responsibility is still to raise resilient children.

  • To teach them humility.
  • To help them respect nature, respect food, and respect effort.

We have to help them build empathy, learn discipline, handle failure, and eventually discover their own passion, their own jam. The curriculum may shape the learning environment, but the home still shapes the human being.

Final Thought

I do not think the future belongs exclusively to IB, Cambridge, CBSE, ICSE, NEP, or SEP. I think the future belongs to education systems that successfully combine academic rigor, communication, creativity, adaptability, emotional resilience, critical thinking, experiential learning, and affordability.

The real challenge is not identifying the ideal system. The real challenge is making it accessible for every child, not just the families who can afford premium alternatives.

And until that happens, many parents will continue doing what parents always do: trying to build the missing guardrails ourselves at home.

That specific, angry shade of red that glows from a dashboard at 2:03 AM. It’s the color of a CPU spike. The color of a failed health check. The color of a pager duty alert piercing through a silent house.

For the first ten years of my career, my life was defined by that red light.

I was the “fixer.” When the board went red, I woke up. I drank coffee. I dug through logs. I stitched together clues while my heart raced, praying I could turn the red back to green before the customers noticed or the CTO called.

My tools told me what was red. But they never told me why.

I was trapped in a cycle of blind automation. We had built pipelines to deploy code faster, but we hadn’t built the intelligence to understand what happened when it broke. I was the manual glue holding a high-speed system together.

title: When AI Stopped Watching and Started Acting
dek: How DevOps is quietly shifting from reactive to predictive , and what I’ve learned along the way
heroCaption: AI didn’t take over incident response. It took over the part that wore us out. The rest? Still ours.
body:
How DevOps is quietly shifting from reactive to predictive , and what I’ve learned along the way

Mid-sprint. Slack lights up. Payment service latency above SLO. Critical.

Everyone on the call goes quiet. You can hear the context-switching happen in real time , tabs opening, terminals firing up, someone already grepping logs before the incident channel is even named.

The system detected the problem. The human-me-had to figure out what it meant.

That used to be the deal. And for years, I accepted it.

But over the past couple of years, something has shifted in how I think about AI/ML in DevOps. Not the theory of it. The actual, practical experience of watching these systems evolve from dashboards that surface noise, to agents that reason through it, to pipelines that try to prevent it entirely.

AI Agents Took Over 75% of My Team’s Work. Here’s the Surprising Upside
How AI agents transformed 75% of our team’s workload: surprising productivity gains, collaboration insights, and what…generativeai.pub

This is what I’ve seen, in four parts.

Part 1: Agents That Act, Not Just Advise

The early ML implementations in DevOps were smart observers. They watched your systems, correlated signals, and surfaced explanations backed by data. Not guesses, patterns. That was genuinely useful. Because understanding why something failed, not just that it failed, is what actually moves the needle on response time.

But understanding alone has a ceiling.

The real shift came when AI moved from explaining problems to acting on them. Not blindly, that would be reckless, but purposefully, with memory and context behind every decision.

An AI Agent in a DevOps context isn’t a chatbot. It’s not a script. It’s a purpose-built system that can observe signals across logs, metrics, traces, and deployment history simultaneously. It remembers what happened last time. It knows what worked and what made things worse.

The memory part matters more than people realise. Traditional tools raise alerts and move on. They don’t accumulate knowledge. AI Agents do, using vector databases to store past incidents and retrieval mechanisms to surface relevant history at the right moment. So when something breaks, the agent isn’t starting from scratch. It’s asking: have we seen this before? What resolved it? What’s the safest next step?

Multiple agents can work in coordination, one detecting the anomaly, another checking recent deployments, another estimating blast radius. The outcome isn’t one agent guessing. It’s a converged, confident recommendation.

The most important rule I’ve seen hold up in practice: agents act only when confidence is high. When it’s low, humans are brought in. Autonomy without guardrails isn’t intelligence. It’s a risk dressed up as efficiency.

Part 2: The Alert That Changed

Let me tell you how that live alert feels now, compared to not long ago.

Back then: I was the correlation engine. I dropped everything, pulled dashboards, grepped logs, formed a hypothesis under pressure with incomplete context. The system detected. I figured it out.

Now: before I even switch context, something else has already started working.

The agent ingests the full system snapshot, metrics, logs, traces, deployment metadata, config diffs. It retrieves similar past incidents from memory. It scores confidence. By the time I open the incident channel, I’m not staring at chaos. I’m reviewing a decision tree.

Latency spike correlates with Deployment #742. Similar to Incident #214, resolved via rollback. Connection pool exhaustion confirmed across traces. Confidence: 91%.

Recommended action: rollback deployment, restore pool config, monitor for five minutes.

That’s not magic. That’s structured reasoning applied to a domain I’ve spent years working in, available the moment the alert fires, not after I’ve had time to catch up.

Chrome Extension Ideas That Make Money: 41 Profitable Niches I’d Build in 2026
A founder-level breakdown of the best Chrome extension ideas across productivity, developer tools, shopping, media…blog.stackademic.com

This is what I call Human-on-the-Loop. The system thinks first. I validate. If the confidence is high and the guardrails allow it, the action executes. If confidence drops, it escalates.

The honest truth: AI didn’t take over incident response. It took over the most exhausting part of it, the cognitive burden of correlating signals under pressure. Every incident now becomes training data. Every resolution improves the next one. MTTR drops not because we type faster, but because we removed the part that wore us out.

Part 3: Trust Is an Architecture Decision

There was a specific moment that made me rethink this.

A script, well-intentioned, reviewed, tested, triggered a cascading failure across three services during a routine deployment. Not a bug. Not bad intent. Just an automation that didn’t understand context. We spent four hours undoing what it did in four seconds.

After that, I drew a hard line. No automation touches production without a human in the decision path. Full stop.

That held for a long time. And it was the right call then.

What changed my thinking wasn’t better models. It was realising that trust in AI systems isn’t a feeling, it’s something you design.

The problem with my hard line was that it put humans back in the exhausting middle. Human-in-the-Loop sounds safe, but in practice it means AI recommends and a tired engineer rubber-stamps at the worst possible moment. That’s not control, that’s theatre.

The real shift came when I started thinking about guardrails as architecture, not policy. Human-on-the-Loop means the AI evaluates risk across multiple dimensions, canary deviation, blast radius, error budget impact, historical similarity, simulates impact, checks policy and ethical constraints, and only acts when a multi-agent consensus clears a defined threshold. If any check fails, it escalates. No exceptions.

That’s constrained autonomy. Not recklessness. Not blind trust.

Where I personally draw the line today: AI can auto-remediate, suppress noise, execute canary rollbacks. Promoting to production stays supervised, not from distrust, but because that decision carries business consequences beyond system health. AI generates the risk model. I validate the outcome.

The notification I receive now reads: Confidence 93%. Ethical guardrails passed.

  • I’m not typing commands.
  • I’m supervising outcomes.

That’s a fundamentally different relationship with automation than the one I had after that cascade. And I think it’s the right one.

The Unfair Advantage: Why Chrome Extensions Are the Ultimate Micro-SaaS for Indie Makers
Forget bloated web apps. The fastest path to recurring revenue is hiding in your browser toolbar. Here’s the playbook.medium.com

Part 4: The Best Incident Response Is the One You Never Need

Here’s the hardest lesson it took me years to fully accept.

We’ve gotten very good at responding to failures. DevOps and SRE teams are genuinely excellent at it. Better monitoring, smarter alerting, faster rollback, the investment shows in recovery times that would’ve seemed impossible a decade ago.

But the loop most teams operate has barely changed:

Deploy → Monitor → Detect → Fix.

No matter how fast the response, we’re still responding after something breaks.

I started asking a different question: what if the pipeline evaluated risk before a change went live? Not just whether tests passed, but real contextual risk, is this change risky in this specific system? Have we seen similar failures with this pattern? What’s the blast radius across dependent services?

This is where AI stops reacting and starts predicting.

I’ve seen pipelines designed to do exactly this, analysing code for historically risky change patterns, mapping dependencies to expose real impact, using observability data to predict expected behaviour. You don’t have to automate blindly. With policy engines like OPA or Kyverno, you can enforce sensible gates: low risk auto-deploys, medium risk goes to canary, high risk or critical vulnerabilities get blocked.

The shift in language is small but significant. From let’s deploy and see what happens to let’s understand what will happen before we deploy.

It changes the conversation in the room. It changes where engineering energy goes. And over time, it changes the culture, from teams that are proud of how fast they respond, to teams that measure how rarely they need to.

AI-powered automation, multiple revenue streams, and zero DevOps headaches. Here’s the exact template I used.medium.com

What I Believe Now

I started this series thinking about AI as a tool that makes DevOps faster. I’ve ended it thinking about AI as something that changes what DevOps teams are for.

The best engineers I know don’t want to drop everything mid-sprint to do correlation work a machine could do better. They want to design systems, make architectural decisions, and apply judgment where it genuinely matters.

AI Agents handle the repeatable. Incident response evolves from reaction to supervision. Trust becomes something you engineer, not something you hope for. And pipelines start thinking before they act.

That’s not a future state. I’ve seen versions of all of this working. The gap between where most teams are and where this is heading is smaller than it looks, and closing faster than most people expect.

If your pipeline could produce a transparent risk assessment before every deployment, with evidence, confidence scores, and a clear recommendation, would you trust it to stop a production deployment on your behalf? What would it take for you to say yes?

title: DevOps Is Not Just Tools: Learning the Tool vs Practising the Job
dek: Certifications and courses can open the door. Real DevOps growth begins when the tool is connected to practice, architecture, ownership and…
body:
Certifications and courses can open the door. Real DevOps growth begins when the tool is connected to practice, architecture, ownership and judgement.

I keep speaking with many enthusiasts who want to explore DevOps, Cloud, AI and the wider IT world. Almost every discussion moves in the same direction: Which certification should I do? Kubernetes? AWS or Azure? Anything in AI?

These are valid questions. Certifications can give structure. Courses can create discipline. Hands-on labs can help you get past the first fear of a new tool.

Yes, you can learn Terraform. You can learn Kubernetes. You can learn Helm. You can learn CI/CD. You can learn dashboards. You can learn AI.

But learning in IT is not only about collecting tools, commands or certificates. Tools tell you what is possible. Practice teaches you when to use them, how to connect them, and what can go wrong when real people depend on the system.

That thought process is what makes an engineer different. The approach matters as much as the tool.

The first level of learning usually explains how a tool works. Real delivery work asks whether that tool can be used safely inside a system with teams, environments, approvals, failures, security and business impact.

The basic exercise asks: Can you deploy this application?

The job asks: Can this application be delivered safely, repeatedly and with enough confidence?

Those are not the same question.

Terraform: From Provisioning to Blast Radius

At the beginning, Terraform looks simple. You write a configuration file, configure a provider, create a VPC, add subnets, run terraform apply, and the infrastructure is ready.

That foundation matters. Without it, the larger conversation is only theory.

In real work, Terraform is not only about creating resources. You may be working with remote state. That state may be locked because multiple people or pipelines depend on it. Your module output may be consumed by another team. A small variable change may affect a resource used by a different application.

The stronger question is not only: Can I write Terraform?

The stronger question is: Do I understand the impact of this infrastructure change before I apply it?

That is where DevOps becomes practice, not just syntax.

Helm: From Chart to Release Pattern

Helm may start as one chart, one values file, one namespace and one command. The application starts, and the lab feels complete.

In a working team, the chart may need to support dev, QA, staging, pre-prod and prod. Each environment can have different resource limits, replica counts, ingress rules and secret sources. You may need separate values files. You may need external secret integration. You may need pre-install checks for database migration. You may need health validation before the release is considered successful.

The Helm chart is not the final deliverable.

The real deliverable is a release pattern that works across environments without surprising the team during release.

CI/CD: From Green Status to Delivery Decision

When you first learn CI/CD, the flow feels clean. Code is committed. The pipeline builds. Tests pass. Deployment happens. Everything is green.

But real delivery does not end at a green status.

There may be code scans, artifact scans, approval evidence, Change Request Management records and environment promotion rules. Some changes may be allowed to move automatically. Some may need manual judgement because they deviate from the standard path.

A useful pipeline is not just automation.

It is a decision flow. It should help the team understand whether the change is safe enough to move forward.

Observability: From Dashboard to Actionable Context

Early observability learning often starts with Prometheus and Grafana. You install the tools. You open the dashboard. CPU, memory and request graphs start moving.

That is a useful beginning, but dashboards are not the goal.

In real jobs, the bigger questions are practical: What should alert? Who should receive the alert? Is the alert connected to user impact? Are logs and traces available when someone starts troubleshooting? Can the team understand what changed before the issue started?

A dashboard can show data. Observability should create actionable context.

The goal is not to stare at graphs. The goal is to understand system behaviour quickly enough to protect users.

The Real Pattern

This pattern appears across most DevOps tools.

Most learning starts with the tool in isolation. Real jobs ask you to use the tool inside a system. That system includes people, process, architecture, security, compliance, release strategy, ownership and recovery.

This is why DevOps is not only about tools.

  • DevOps is practice.
  • DevOps is architecture design.
  • DevOps is operational thinking.
  • DevOps is knowing when automation is enough and when human judgement is needed.

A Better Way to Keep Learning

Finish the courses. Complete the labs. They are important.

But do not stop there.

After the basic version works, make the project harder.

Take one simple application and create three environments. Add different configuration for each environment. Add a basic CI/CD pipeline. Add a scan report. Add a manual approval for production. Add one failure scenario and practise rollback.

  • You do not need a large enterprise platform to start thinking like this.
  • You just need to move beyond the happy path.

That is where real learning begins.

I am open to discussions.

When you moved from learning mode to real work, what surprised you the most: tools, process, architecture, approvals or troubleshooting?

           "ec2.amazonaws.com",
           "ecs.amazonaws.com",
           "ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com",
           "application-autoscaling.amazonaws.com" 
         ]
       },
       "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
     }
   ]
 }

Optional: Auto Scaling

  • User can also configure Amazon ECS services to use Service Auto Scaling. Service Auto Scaling policies adjust your Amazon ECS service’s desired count up or down in response to Cloud-watch alarms (e.g. tracking the CPU utilization of an Amazon ECS service, or tracking a custom metric) or on a schedule (e.g. scale up on Monday, scale down on Friday).
  • Configure scaling policies on your Amazon ECS services using the Application Auto Scaling APIs or in the Amazon ECS console, outside of Spinnaker. When deploying a new server group in Spinnaker, you can copy these scaling policies from the previous service group by enabling the “copy the previous server group’s auto-scaling policies” option.

Add ECS Account and Enable ECS Provider

  • Below command allows user to add ECS account to Spinnaker
hal config provider ecs account add ecs-account-name --aws-account aws-account-name

Note: From the above Command ‘ecs-account-name is the AWS ECS Account Name and the ‘aws-account-name’ is the AWS EC2 Account Name

  • Below command allows user to enable ECS account to Spinnaker.
hal config provider ecs enable

Note: Ensure to have AWS account enabled before enabling ECS on Spinnaker.

Step by Step Instructions to Create Pipeline with ECS Stage

  • This pipeline includes 3 stages, Build(Jenkins), Bake(AWS EC2) and Deploy(ECS)
  • Create an Application and Click on Pipelines to create a Pipeline
  • Click on ‘Configure a new pipeline’
  • Pipeline Name as per your requirement
  • To add stage to deploy your application. Before adding Deploy stage it is mandatory for ECS Deploy to Bake/Find Image from Cluster/Find Image from Tags. In this blog we will exploring about Building Artifacts and Baking Immutable Image to deploy into Fargate Cluster.
  • Click on ‘Add Stage’ Select ‘Jenkins’ and add your Jenkins Job as required and Click on ‘Save Changes’.
  • Now, Click on ‘Add Stage’ and select ‘Bake’. Fill up all the mandatory as done on AWS EC2 Bake Stage.
  • Finally, Click on ‘Add Stage’ and select ‘Deploy’ then Click on ‘Add Server Group’ under ‘Deploy Configuration’.
  • Select ‘ECS’ as Cloudprovider and Click on ‘Next’.

Now, start filling up all the mandatory fields like,

  • ECS Account
  • Region
  • Cluster Name
  • Enter Stack & Detail(Optional)
  • Strategy — In this scenario i have user Red/Black(Disables all previous server groups in the Cluster as soon as new servergroup passes health check).
  • Network Mode — awsvpc — As this document refers with ‘Fargate’ it is mandatory to have networking mode as awsvpc.
  • Target Group
  • Target Container Port
  • Container Image, CPU & Memory for the Image
  • Launch Type, Desired Capacity — Min & Max
  • IAM Instance Profile, Health Check Grace Period and other fields as required.

Once, done with filling up all the fields in ‘Deploy’ Click on ‘Done’ and ‘Save Changes’. With this, you are all set to execute your AWS ECS with AWS Fargate Pipeline on Spinnaker.

title: How to Integrate AWS with Spinnaker
body:
Overview

  • Assuming that you have Spinnaker Installed, we will explore about Integrating AWS with Spinnaker in this Blog.
  • In AWS, an EC2 is used to launch as many VM’s as we need, to configure security and networking, and to manage storage.
  • In Spinnaker, AWS plays almost the same role when user configures AWS as a Cloud Provider.
  • There are two methods to configure AWS as Cloudprovider,
  1. By using AWS Console
  2. By using AWS CLI
  • In this document we will explore the integration process using AWS Console

Steps to Setup EC2 with Spinnaker

  • Steps to create Managing Account
  1. Navigate to Console > CloudFormation and select your preferred region.
  2. Click here to Download the template locally.
  3. Search for ‘SpinnakerInstanceProfileArn’ and comment out the line.
  4. (Optional). Add additional managed account as shown on line 158 in the SpinnakerAssumeRolePolicy section of the downloaded template file.
  5. Execute the below to create the CloudFormation Stack
    - Create Stack > Upload a template to Amazon S3 > Browse to template you downloaded in Step-2 above > Next
    - Enter Stack Name as ‘spinnaker-managing-infrastructure-setup’, Click on the dropdown ‘UseAccessKeyForAuthentication’ and select true to get the Access and Secret Key.
    - Then follow the prompts on screen and click on create the stack.
  6. Once the stack is select the stack you created in Step-3 > Outputs and note the values(AccessKeyId, Secret, ManagingAccountID & AuthArn). These values are mandatory for subsequent configurations.
  • Steps to Create Managed Account.
  1. Navigate to Console > CloudFormation and select your preferred region.
  2. Click here to Download the template locally.
  3. Creating the CloudFormation Stack
    - Create Stack > Upload a template to Amazon S3 > Browse to template you downloaded in Step-2 above > Next
    - Enter Stack Name as ‘spinnaker-managed-infrastructure-setup’ and follow the prompts on screen to create the stack
    - Enter AuthArn and ManagingAccountId as the value noted above and follow the prompts on screen to create the stack

Steps to Create IAM Role for EC2

  1. Navigate to Console > IAM > Roles
  2. Click on Create New Role, select EC2 and name it as per requirement(eg. ec2-instance)
  3. Search for the below policies
    - AmazonEC2FullAccess
    - spinnakerAssumeRolePolicy
    - baseiampolicy
    - AutoScalingFullAccess
    - PowerUserAccess
  4. Click on Review and Submit to Create.
  5. Now Edit the newly created role and click on TrustRelationships and add the below JSON entry
{
   "Version": "2012-10-17",
   "Statement": [
     {
       "Effect": "Allow",
       "Principal": {
         "Service": [
           "ec2.amazonaws.com" 
         ]
       },
       "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
     }
   ]
 }

Steps to Create “Spinnaker AssumeRole Policy”

  1. Navigate to Console > IAM > Policies.
  2. Click on Create New Policy, click on JSON and add the below code.
  3. Name the policy as “Spinnaker AssumeRole Policy”.
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:iam::<AWSAccountID>:role/spinnakerManaged",
                "arn:aws:iam::<AWSAccountID>:role/spinnakerManaged"
            ],
            "Effect": "Allow"
        }
    ]
}

Steps to configure AWS EC2 using AWS CLI

Managing Account creation using

  • Execute the below command to use AccessKey and Secret to run Spinnaker
curl https://d3079gxvs8ayeg.cloudfront.net/templates/managing.yaml
------------------------------------------------------------------echo "Optionally add Managing account to the file downloaded as shown on line 158 in the SpinnakerAssumeRolePolicy section of the downloaded file."
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name spinnaker-managing-infrastructure-setup --template-file managing.yaml \ --parameter-overrides UseAccessKeyForAuthentication=true --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM --region us-east-1
  • Execute the below command to use InstanceProfile run Spinnaker
curl https://d3079gxvs8ayeg.cloudfront.net/templates/managing.yaml
------------------------------------------------------------------
echo "Optionally add Managing account to the file downloaded as shown on line 158 in the SpinnakerAssumeRolePolicy section of the downloaded file."
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name spinnaker-managing-infrastructure-setup --template-file managing.yaml \
 --parameter-overrides UseAccessKeyForAuthentication=false --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM --region us-east-1

Managed Account Creation

  • Note: These steps need to be carried out for the managing account as well.
curl https://d3079gxvs8ayeg.cloudfront.net/templates/managed.yaml
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name spinnaker-managed-infrastructure-setup --template-file managed.yaml \
 --parameter-overrides AuthArn=FROM_ABOVE ManagingAccountId=FROM_ABOVE --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM --region us-east-1

Configure Halyard with AccessKeys

  • These steps need to be executed only if you selected UseAccessKeyForAuthentication as true in Option-1 or Option-2 above
ACCESSKEYID=12345678910(Update this with your Access Key)
hal config provider aws edit --access-key-id ${ACCESSKEYID} \
--secret-access-key#do not supply the key here, you will be prompted 
hal config provider aws bakery edit --aws-access-key ${ACCESSKEYID} \
--aws-secret-key # do not supply the key here, you will be prompted

Configure Halyard to add AWS account

  • Execute the below command to add AWS EC2 Account
$AWS_ACCOUNT_NAME={name for AWS account in Spinnaker, e.g. my-aws-account}
 hal config provider aws account add $AWS_ACCOUNT_NAME \
     --account-id ${ACCOUNT_ID} \
     --assume-role role/spinnakerManaged \
     --regions us-east-1
  • Execute the below command to Enable AWS
hal config provider aws enable
  • Now, restart Spinnaker to see the changes reflecting on your spinnaker
hal deploy apply

Now you have successfully configured AWS as a cloud provider in Spinnaker.
